_note: Real, public postmortems. Summaries are OUR OWN words (<= 60 words), written after reading each page on 2026-10-15. published_at is the page's publication date, or the incident date when the page shows none. Loaded into every tenant graph by seed.load.

rc:cache-ttl-thundering-herd: Cached data expires, is dropped or is judged invalid everywhere at once, so every client refetches from one shared store and overloads it.
rc:bad-config-push: An invalid or wrong configuration was rolled out widely, fast, without enough validation or canarying.
rc:retry-storm: Clients retry or reconnect without backoff and jitter, so a recovering dependency is overloaded again.
rc:dns-bgp-misconfiguration: Names stop resolving or routes are withdrawn, so healthy services become unreachable.
rc:hidden-dependency: A failure spreads through a dependency that was not mapped or not treated as critical, often including the tools needed to recover.
rc:database-failover: A primary fails or is replaced and failover, replication or recovery does not behave as expected.
rc:capacity-limit: Growth or a change pushes a component past a fixed limit (threads, file handles, feature count, network capacity) and it fails.
rc:operator-error: A manual command with a wrong input or on the wrong host does far more than intended.

postmortems.title: Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019
postmortems.summary: A new WAF managed rule shipped to every location at once. Its regular expression backtracked badly and pinned the CPUs that serve web traffic, and a CPU safeguard had been removed by mistake earlier. Disabling the WAF globally restored traffic; it came back once the safeguard was reinstated.

postmortems.title: Cloudflare outage on November 18, 2025
postmortems.summary: A database permissions change made the job that builds the Bot Management feature file emit duplicate rows, roughly doubling the file. The proxy had a fixed cap on features, so the oversized file made it fail with 5xx errors. Stopping the file's propagation and shipping a known-good copy fixed it.

postmortems.title: More details about the October 4 outage
postmortems.summary: A maintenance command meant to assess backbone capacity disconnected the whole backbone; an audit tool bug let it through. DNS servers then withdrew their BGP routes, so Meta vanished from the internet. Remote tooling was down too, so engineers restored the network on site and brought load back gradually.

postmortems.title: Summary of the Amazon S3 Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region
postmortems.summary: While debugging billing, an engineer ran a capacity-removal command with a wrong input and took out far more S3 servers than intended, including index and placement subsystems. Their restart was slow at that scale. AWS made the tool remove capacity slowly and refuse to go below each subsystem's minimum.

postmortems.title: Summary of the Amazon Kinesis Event in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region
postmortems.summary: Adding front-end capacity to Kinesis pushed every front-end server past an OS thread limit, so they could not build their shard maps. Services that quietly relied on Kinesis, such as Cognito and CloudWatch, failed with it. Removing the new capacity and slowly restarting the fleet restored service.

postmortems.title: Slack's Incident on 2-22-22
postmortems.summary: A rolling Consul agent upgrade restarted memcached nodes at peak and they came back empty. Cache misses turned an expensive membership query into scatter queries across every database shard, and the overloaded database stopped the cache from refilling. Throttling client boots and fixing the query restored service.

postmortems.title: October 21 post-incident analysis
postmortems.summary: A 43-second network partition during routine maintenance made the MySQL failover tool promote primaries in another region. Both sites then held writes the other lacked, so failing back safely was impossible. GitHub paused webhooks and Pages, restored from backups, resynced replicas and drained the backlog over about a day.

postmortems.title: Root cause analysis: significantly elevated error rates on 2019-07-10
postmortems.summary: A database cluster's primary failed and the cluster could not elect a replacement, because of a fault in a database version upgraded months earlier. Restarting nodes forced an election. A second degradation came from a rolled-back election setting interacting with a recent configuration change, fixed by correcting the configuration.

postmortems.title: Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region
postmortems.summary: A race between two automated DNS updaters let a stale plan overwrite a newer one, and a clean-up job then deleted it, leaving DynamoDB's regional endpoint with an empty DNS record. Clients could not resolve it. Engineers repaired DNS by hand and paused the automation worldwide until safeguards exist.

postmortems.title: Summary of the AWS Service Event in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region
postmortems.summary: An automated scaling activity triggered a surge of connections from internal clients that overwhelmed the devices between AWS's internal and main networks. A latent bug stopped those clients from backing off, so retries kept the congestion going. AWS stopped the scaling, rerouted internal DNS traffic, added capacity and fixed the back-off.

postmortems.title: Summary of June 8 outage
postmortems.summary: A software release weeks earlier carried a latent bug that only a particular customer configuration could trigger. When one customer pushed a valid change matching it, most of the edge network returned errors. Fastly disabled that configuration within the hour and then shipped a permanent fix.

postmortems.title: Multiple GCP products are experiencing Service issues
postmortems.summary: A policy with blank fields replicated globally within seconds and hit new, unflagged Service Control code without error handling, which crashed in a loop. A kill switch disabled the path quickly, but restarting tasks without randomized backoff overloaded the Spanner backend in a large region, stretching recovery there by hours.

postmortems.title: Cloudflare outage on June 21, 2022
postmortems.summary: A change to BGP advertisement policies on spine routers reordered the terms so a reject-all rule ran before the site-local ones. Nineteen busy data centers stopped advertising their prefixes and went dark. Engineers regained access through backup paths and reverted the change on each router.

postmortems.title: Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 Incident on July 14, 2025
postmortems.summary: A not-yet-live service had been wrongly tied to the 1.1.1.1 resolver's IP prefixes weeks before. An unrelated change to it triggered a global configuration refresh that shrank the resolver's topology to one offline site, so the prefixes were withdrawn everywhere for about an hour. Reverting the configuration fixed it.

postmortems.title: Google Cloud Networking Incident #19009
postmortems.summary: Maintenance in one location set off automation that, through two small misconfigurations and a bug, descheduled network control-plane jobs in several sites. After a fail-static period, BGP routes were withdrawn and capacity in several US regions collapsed. Stopping the automation and rebuilding the control plane's configuration restored it.

postmortems.title: Roblox Return to Service
postmortems.summary: A newly enabled Consul streaming feature and a BoltDB performance bug made Roblox's single Consul cluster unhealthy. Service discovery, scheduling, secrets and even monitoring all depended on it, so the platform was down for about 73 hours. Disabling streaming and compacting BoltDB recovered it; critical services later got separate clusters.

postmortems.title: Slack's Outage on January 4th 2021
postmortems.summary: The first workday of the year brought a traffic surge that an AWS Transit Gateway could not scale for quickly, so it dropped packets. Autoscaling then failed because the provisioning service depended on the same degraded network and hit file and quota limits. AWS raised the gateway's capacity by hand.

postmortems.title: Postmortem of database outage of January 31
postmortems.summary: Load made a PostgreSQL replica fall too far behind. While rebuilding it, an engineer wiped the primary's data directory instead, and backups had been failing unnoticed. GitLab restored from a six-hour-old staging snapshot, lost some data, and added snapshot, backup-monitoring and replication runbook fixes.

postmortems.title: 2023-03-08 Incident: Infrastructure connectivity issue affecting multiple regions
postmortems.summary: An automatic systemd security update reached many VMs at once. When systemd-networkd restarted on running nodes it deleted routes owned by the Cilium container network, taking the nodes offline; freshly booted nodes were fine. Datadog disabled that update channel and told networkd to leave existing routes alone.

postmortems.title: More Details on Today's Outage
postmortems.summary: A change to a stored configuration value made an automated checker treat it as invalid, so every client tried to fix its cached copy by querying one database cluster. Errors were read as invalid values and caused more cache deletions, a feedback loop. The site was taken down to stop traffic, then restored gradually.

postmortems.title: Billing Incident Post-Mortem: Breakdown, Analysis and Root Cause
postmortems.summary: A network blip disconnected the billing Redis replicas; on reconnect they all asked for a full resync and overloaded the primary. Restarting the primary loaded a wrong configuration, losing the in-memory balances, so auto-recharge charged customer cards repeatedly. Billing was shut down and affected customers were credited.
